title: Korach: the man who went home (Sanhedrin 109b)
hookLine: On ben Peleth vanishes from the rebellion; the Talmud says his wife talked him out of it

cards: Read the first verse of the Korach story slowly and you'll find a roll call. Korach. Dathan and Abiram.
And one more: On, the son of Peleth. He's right there at the start of the rebellion, named with the leaders. Then he's gone.
When the trouble comes to its terrible end, Korach, Dathan and Abiram are all named again. On never appears again, anywhere in the Bible. Readers noticed the gap long ago.
What happened to the fourth man? The Talmud has an answer, and it's a story about a kitchen-table conversation.

teach.h: WHAT DO YOU GET OUT OF THIS?
teach.b: The story is in the Talmud, in tractate Sanhedrin; here it is in paraphrase. On's wife asks him a simple question: what do you get out of this? If Moses stays the leader, you're a follower.

If Korach becomes the leader, you're still a follower. On admits she's right, but says he's stuck: he was in the meeting, he gave his word, they're counting on him. So she says, in effect, leave it to me.

teach.h: SHE SITS AT THE TENT'S ENTRANCE.
teach.b: She gives him wine, he falls asleep inside the tent, and she sits at the entrance, in a way that makes the men coming to fetch him turn back. By the time he wakes, the rebellion is over, and he's alive.

teach.h: A WISE WOMAN BUILDS HER HOUSE.
teach.b: The Talmud reads a verse from Proverbs over the scene: every wise woman builds her house, but the foolish one tears it down with her own hands. The wise woman is On's wife. And the foolish one?
The same passage says Korach's wife egged him on, feeding his resentment of Moses. Two homes, two conversations, two endings. A few things are worth noticing.

teach.h: THE TORAH IS SILENT; THE TALMUD ANSWERS.
teach.b: The Torah itself says nothing about any of this; the Talmud is answering a silence in the text. Her argument isn't about who's right. It's about him: this fight isn't yours, and it won't give you what you think.
And On's problem, but I already gave my word, is one plenty of people know. Sometimes the bravest thing is letting someone who loves you talk you down from a fight you joined too fast.

how: The story of On ben Peleth and his wife is a well-known Talmudic teaching that is often told when the portion of Korach is read in synagogue in early summer.

o: a story the Talmud tells about Moses' wife
a verse from Proverbs about a wise wife
the rebellion one man left by staying home

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.
p: named at the start, then gone

s: the Torah tells us On's wife saved him
the Torah only names On once. the story of his wife comes from the Talmud, Sanhedrin 109b.
On's wife argued that he'd be a follower either way
if Moses leads, you follow; if Korach leads, you still follow.
On is named again when the rebellion ends
Korach, Dathan and Abiram are named again. On never reappears.

games.q: you're On. you joined the rebels, you gave your word, and your wife says this fight will get you nothing. what do you do?
o: keep your word to the rebels.
let her handle it, and stay home.
go to Moses and switch sides loudly.
games.why: in the Talmud's story, he stays home and sleeps while she keeps the rebels away from the tent. he lives; the rebellion doesn't.

practice: Think of the person in your life who's good at asking what you actually get out of this, a partner, a friend, a sibling, an old teacher, and picture their face.
Imagine telling them about one fight you're in, or tempted to join, and let their question sit with you without defending yourself. If you're grateful for them, let yourself feel it.

wordCard.voice: Korach. The rebellion that started with four named men, and ended, the Talmud says, with one of them asleep safely at home.

orig.note: Hebrew: On, son of Peleth, named in Numbers 16:1 and never again.

carryVoice: Your line: she saved him. One honest question at home ended a war outside. Four hundred fifty-four days now.
